solution.faster: List the admissible sizes first (0, 3, 6), then look each binomial coefficient up in the 8th row of Pascal's triangle: 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1.
solution.takeaway: “Cardinality divisible by k” is always a sum of binomial coefficients over the admissible sizes.

questions.question: Which one of the following sets is uncountable?
options: the set of all algebraic real numbers

solution.concept: Countable sets are those that can be listed; ℚ, ℤ × ℤ and the algebraic numbers all have an enumeration, while the power set of ℕ cannot be listed by Cantor's theorem.
steps: ℚ is countable: the fractions can be listed along the diagonals of a grid.
ℤ × ℤ is a countable product of countable sets, hence countable.

The algebraic numbers are the roots of non-zero polynomials with integer coefficients; there are countably many such polynomials, each with finitely many roots, so the algebraic numbers are countable.
|P(ℕ)| = 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₀ by Cantor's theorem, so P(ℕ) is uncountable.
why_wrong: (A) ℚ is countable, though it is dense in ℝ; density and countability are independent.
(B) A finite product of countable sets is countable.
(D) “Algebraic” sounds restrictive, but the algebraic numbers are countable — it is the transcendental ones that are uncountable.
solution.misconception: Density is confused with uncountability. ℚ is dense in ℝ yet countable; between any two reals there are only countably many rationals but uncountably many reals.
solution.faster: Remember the two cardinalities the syllabus tests: ℵ₀ for anything listable (integers, rationals, pairs, finite strings, algebraic numbers) and 2^ℵ₀ for anything involving all subsets or all real numbers.
solution.takeaway: Listable ⇒ countable. “All subsets of ℕ” and “all real numbers” are the standard uncountable sets.

questions.question: Let A be an infinite set and let B ⊆ A be finite. Which one of the following is necessarily TRUE?

solution.concept: Removing finitely many elements from an infinite set never changes its cardinality: A − B and A can be put in bijection.
steps: Write A = (A − B) ∪ B; the two parts are disjoint and B is finite, say B = {b₁, …, bₖ}.
Take a countably infinite subset C ⊆ A − B (it exists because A is infinite and only finitely many points were removed).
List C = {c₁, c₂, …} and map cᵢ ↦ c_{i+k}, bⱼ ↦ cⱼ, fixing everything else. This is a bijection from A onto A − B.
Hence |A − B| = |A|.
why_wrong: (B) |A| − |B| is not even meaningful when A is infinite; cardinal arithmetic does not subtract finite numbers from infinite ones like this.
(C) A − B is still infinite, since only finitely many elements were removed.
(D) The cardinality is unchanged, not smaller.
solution.misconception: Treating infinite cardinalities as if they obeyed the arithmetic of natural numbers. For infinite A, |A| − 1 = |A|; subtraction is simply not defined the finite way.
solution.faster: Ask what a finite deletion can do: nothing to the size of an infinite set. That eliminates (B), (C) and (D) at once.
solution.takeaway: Infinite minus finite is the same infinite cardinality.

questions.question: Let S be the set of all infinite subsets of ℕ. The cardinality of S is

solution.concept: All subsets of ℕ number 2^ℵ₀; only countably many of them are finite, and removing countably many elements from an uncountable set leaves an uncountable set of the same cardinality.
steps: |P(ℕ)| = 2^ℵ₀.
The finite subsets of ℕ form a countable family: for each n there are only C(k, n) subsets of size n, a countable union of finite sets.
So S = P(ℕ) − {finite subsets} has cardinality 2^ℵ₀ − ℵ₀ = 2^ℵ₀.
why_wrong: (A) ℵ₀ is the size of the finite subsets, not of the infinite ones.
(C) 2^(2^ℵ₀) is the size of P(P(ℕ)), one level too high.
(D) S contains, for instance, every set ℕ − {k}, which is already infinitely many distinct infinite subsets.
solution.misconception: “Infinite subsets are hard to describe, so there must be few of them.” The opposite is true: the infinite subsets are almost all of P(ℕ), and the finite ones are a countable dust.
solution.faster: Removing a countable set from an uncountable set changes nothing. Locate the small part, subtract it, keep the cardinality.
solution.takeaway: Countable subsets are a negligible part of P(ℕ); the complement keeps the full cardinality 2^ℵ₀.

questions.question: For any sets A and B, the set A − (A − B) equals

solution.concept: Rewrite difference as intersection with a complement and simplify: A − X = A ∩ X′.
steps: A − B = A ∩ B′, so A − (A − B) = A ∩ (A ∩ B′)′.
By De Morgan, (A ∩ B′)′ = A′ ∪ B.
Distribute: A ∩ (A′ ∪ B) = (A ∩ A′) ∪ (A ∩ B) = ∅ ∪ (A ∩ B) = A ∩ B.
why_wrong: (B) A − B is the inner set, which was removed; it cannot survive.
(C) B − A shares no element with A, so it cannot be the answer.
(D) A ∪ B includes elements of B outside A, which the double difference never contains.
solution.misconception: “Removing the removal puts everything back” is the natural but wrong intuition. Removing A − B from A leaves exactly the part of A that was in B.
solution.faster: Test with A = {1, 2}, B = {2, 3}: A − B = {1} and A − {1} = {2} = A ∩ B.
solution.takeaway: Double difference is not the identity map; A − (A − B) = A ∩ B.

questions.question: For any sets A, B, C, the set (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ B′ ∩ C) equals

solution.concept: Factor out the common A, then simplify the bracket with the absorption identity B ∪ (B′ ∩ C) = B ∪ C.
steps: Factor: (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ B′ ∩ C) = A ∩ (B ∪ (B′ ∩ C)).
Distribute the bracket: B ∪ (B′ ∩ C) = (B ∪ B′) ∩ (B ∪ C) = U ∩ (B ∪ C) = B ∪ C.
Therefore the set is A ∩ (B ∪ C).
why_wrong: (A) A ∩ B ∩ C is far too small: it drops the whole of A ∩ B.
(B) A ∪ (B ∩ C) adds elements outside A, which neither term contains.
(D) (A ∪ B) ∩ C requires membership in C, which the first term does not.
solution.misconception: Students reach for A ∩ B ∩ C because the second term looks like a narrowing of the first. The union of the two terms is what widens the result to all of A ∩ (B ∪ C).
solution.faster: Take A = U = {1, 2, 3}, B = {1}, C = {2}. The expression gives {1, 2}, which matches only A ∩ (B ∪ C).
solution.takeaway: Difference-flavoured terms usually simplify by factoring out the common set and applying B ∪ (B′ ∩ C) = B ∪ C.

questions.question: Starting from two sets A and B and applying ∪, ∩ and complement (relative to U = A ∪ B) any number of times, at most how many distinct sets can be produced?

solution.concept: Two sets cut the universe into four disjoint regions; every set built from A, B by the Boolean operations is a union of some of those regions, so there are at most 2⁴ = 16 of them.
steps: The four Venn regions are A ∩ B, A ∩ B′, A′ ∩ B, A′ ∩ B′; they partition U.
Any expression built with ∪, ∩, ′ is a union of whole regions — it never splits a region, because the generators are constant on each region.
So each obtainable set is described by choosing a subset of the four regions: at most 2⁴ = 16 sets.
All 16 really occur (the empty set, the four regions, the four unions of two regions, …), so the bound is attained.
why_wrong: (A) 4 is the number of Venn regions, not the number of sets built from them.
(B) 8 would be the answer for a single generator with a universe of three regions.
(D) 32 = 2⁵ counts a fifth region that does not exist for two sets.
solution.misconception: Counting expressions instead of counting the distinct sets they denote. Infinitely many expressions collapse onto 16 sets, which is why a finite bound exists at all.
solution.faster: Memorise the formula: n generators give 2^{2ⁿ} sets in the free Boolean algebra — 4 for one, 16 for two, 256 for three.
solution.takeaway: The Boolean algebra on n generators has 2^{2ⁿ} elements; for n = 2 that is 16.

questions.question: In a group of 40 students, 25 play cricket, 20 play football and 10 play both. How many play neither game?

solution.concept: Two-set inclusion-exclusion gives the size of the union; the answer is the complement of that union inside the group.
steps: Students playing neither = 40 − 35 = 5.
why_wrong: (A) 0 would mean the union fills the group, i.e. |C ∪ F| = 40, which it does not.
(C) 10 is the size of the overlap, not of the complement.
(D) 15 = 25 − 10, the number playing cricket only.
solution.misconception: Adding 25 + 20 = 45 and concluding that 5 students were double counted is correct arithmetic but answers a different question. The overlap is given as 10, not 5.
solution.faster: Union first, complement second — always in that order for “neither” questions.
solution.takeaway: “Neither” = total − union, and the union needs inclusion-exclusion.

questions.question: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 are divisible by exactly one of 3 and 5?

solution.concept: Multiples of 3 form a set, multiples of 5 another; “exactly one” means the symmetric difference, counted as |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B| with A ∩ B = multiples of 15.
steps: ⌊200/3⌋ = 66 multiples of 3.
⌊200/5⌋ = 40 multiples of 5.
⌊200/15⌋ = 13 multiples of both.
Exactly one: (66 − 13) + (40 − 13) = 53 + 27 = 80.
why_wrong: (A) 53 counts only the multiples of 3 that are not multiples of 5.
(B) 66 is the total number of multiples of 3, including the shared ones.
(D) 93 = 66 + 40 − 13 is the union — divisible by 3 or 5, which includes multiples of 15.
solution.misconception: “Exactly one” is routinely read as “at least one”. The union counts multiples of 15 once; symmetric difference excludes them altogether.
solution.faster: Exactly one of two = union − intersection = 93 − 13 = 80. Same number, one line less.
solution.takeaway: Exactly-one-of-two = |A ∪ B| − |A ∩ B|.

questions.question: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 500 are divisible by exactly two of the numbers 2, 3 and 5?

solution.concept: Sum the pairwise intersections, then subtract three times the triple intersection, because an element in all three sets is counted in all three pairwise terms but must not be counted at all.
steps: Sum of pairwise intersections: 83 + 50 + 33 = 166.
|2 ∧ 3 ∧ 5| = ⌊500/30⌋ = 16; these 16 elements appear in all three pairwise terms and must be removed.
Exactly two = 166 − 3·16 = 166 − 48 = 118.
why_wrong: (A) 102 subtracts the triple intersection twice instead of three times.
(C) 134 subtracts the triple intersection only once.
(D) 150 is close to the sum of pairwise intersections with the triple intersection ignored in a different way; it does not correspond to “exactly two”.
solution.misconception: The coefficient of the triple intersection is 3, not 1 or 2. Each element divisible by 30 lies in all three pairwise intersections, so it must be cancelled three times.
solution.faster: Exactly-two = (sum of pairwise intersections) − 3·(triple). For exactly-one it is (sum of singles) − 2·(sum of pairwise) + 3·(triple).
solution.takeaway: Learn the coefficients: exactly one uses 1, −2, 3; exactly two uses 0, 1, −3.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. How many elements does the set P(A) × {x, y} have?

solution.concept: The product rule multiplies cardinalities, and |P(A)| = 2^{|A|}.
steps: |A| = 3, so |P(A)| = 2³ = 8.
The second factor has 2 elements.
Therefore |P(A) × {x, y}| = 8 · 2 = 16.
why_wrong: (A) 6 = 3 · 2 uses |A| instead of |P(A)|.
(B) 8 is |P(A)| alone, forgetting the second factor.
(C) 12 = 8 + 4 or 3 · 4: neither the product rule nor a correct sum.
solution.misconception: Reading P(A) as A. The power set has 2³ = 8 members, not 3.
solution.faster: Cartesian product sizes always multiply; get the size of each factor right first.
solution.takeaway: A product of sets is counted by the product rule, with |P(A)| = 2^{|A|}.

questions.question: How many partitions of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} have exactly three blocks?

solution.concept: The number of partitions of an n-element set into exactly k blocks is the Stirling number of the second kind S(n, k), computed by S(n,k) = k·S(n−1,k) + S(n−1,k−1).
steps: Base values: S(5, 2) = 2⁴ − 1 = 15 and S(5, 3) = 25.
Recurrence: S(6, 3) = 3·S(5, 3) + S(5, 2) = 3·25 + 15.
= 75 + 15 = 90.
why_wrong: (A) 15 = S(5, 2), the two-block count for a five-element set.
(B) 31 is S(6, 4) + S(6, 3) partially added — an arithmetic slip, not a valid count.
(C) 45 is half of 90 and comes from treating the three blocks as distinguishable.
solution.misconception: Counting ordered triples of blocks instead of partitions overcounts by 3! = 6 — the blocks of a partition are an unordered collection.
solution.faster: Learn the Stirling triangle: row 6 is 1, 31, 90, 65, 15, 1. The third entry is 90.
solution.takeaway: Exactly k blocks = S(n,k); total partitions = Bell number B(n).

questions.question: How many ordered pairs (A, B) of subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} satisfy A ∩ B = ∅?

solution.concept: Independently for each element there are three legal placements — in A only, in B only, or in neither — and disjointness forbids the fourth.
steps: Fix an element x of the 5-element ground set.
Disjointness allows exactly three placements: x ∈ A, x ∈ B, or x ∉ A ∪ B. The placement x ∈ A ∩ B is forbidden.
Choices for different elements are independent, so the count is 3⁵ = 243.
why_wrong: (A) 125 = 5³ mixes the roles of the base and the exponent.
(C) 252 = C(10, 5), which counts something entirely different.
(D) 1024 = 2^{10} = 4⁵ counts all pairs (A, B) with no disjointness condition.
solution.misconception: Starting from 4⁵ = 1024 and trying to subtract the non-disjoint pairs is messy and error-prone; counting the three allowed placements per element is immediate.
solution.faster: Two sets with a disjointness constraint = ternary choice per element = 3ⁿ. Drop the constraint and it becomes 4ⁿ.
solution.takeaway: Constraints that exclude one combination per element turn a 4ⁿ count into a 3ⁿ count.

questions.question: For sets A and B, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If A ⊆ B, then P(A) ⊆ P(B).
|P(A × B)| = |P(A)| · |P(B)| for all finite A, B.

solution.concept: The power set converts ⊆ into ∈ and preserves intersections, but it does not preserve unions, and its size does not multiply.
steps: (A) If every element of A lies in B, every subset of A is also a subset of B, so P(A) ⊆ P(B). TRUE.
(B) X ∈ P(A ∩ B) means X ⊆ A ∩ B, which holds exactly when X ⊆ A and X ⊆ B, i.e. X ∈ P(A) ∩ P(B). TRUE.
(C) Take A = {1}, B = {2}. Then {1, 2} ∈ P(A ∪ B) but {1, 2} ∉ P(A) ∪ P(B). FALSE.
(D) |P(A × B)| = 2^{|A|·|B|} while |P(A)| · |P(B)| = 2^{|A|+|B|}. These agree only when |A|·|B| = |A|+|B|, e.g. |A| = |B| = 2 gives 16 ≠ 8. FALSE.
solution.misconception: “The power set of a union is the union of the power sets” feels symmetric and is repeated in notes; the mixed subset {1, 2} is the one-line refutation.
solution.faster: Test any claimed power-set identity with A = {1}, B = {2}; it separates union from intersection immediately.
solution.takeaway: P preserves ∩ and ⊆; it does not preserve ∪ and does not turn products into products.

questions.question: Which of the following claims about countable and uncountable sets are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every infinite subset of ℕ is countably infinite.
If A and B are countably infinite, then A × B is countably infinite.
The union of countably many countable sets is countable.
The set of all real numbers whose decimal expansion uses only the digits 0 and 1 is countable.

solution.concept: The countable sets are closed under subsets, finite products and countable unions; the binary-expansion reals are the standard uncountable exception.
steps: (A) An infinite subset of ℕ can be listed in increasing order, which is an enumeration by ℕ. TRUE.
(B) ℕ × ℕ is countable by the diagonal enumeration, and A × B is in bijection with it. TRUE.
(C) This is the standard countable-union theorem; enumerate the i-th element of the j-th set along the diagonals of the grid. TRUE.
(D) These reals correspond to infinite binary sequences, of which there are 2^ℵ₀ — uncountable. FALSE.
solution.misconception: (D) is tempting because the restriction to two digits feels like a drastic thinning. It is not: the set of infinite binary sequences is still in bijection with P(ℕ).
solution.faster: Two-digit expansions = infinite binary strings = subsets of ℕ, so the size is 2^ℵ₀ at once.
solution.takeaway: Countable is closed under subset, finite product and countable union — but not under power set.

questions.question: For arbitrary sets A, B, C, which of the following identities hold? (Select all that apply.)

solution.concept: De Morgan governs complements of unions and intersections; difference is a masked intersection; symmetric difference is the union minus the overlap.
steps: (A) A ∩ (B ∪ C)′ = A ∩ B′ ∩ C′ = (A ∩ B′) ∩ (A ∩ C′). TRUE.
(B) Take A = {1, 2}, B = {2}, C = {2}. Left side is {1}, right side is {1, 2}. FALSE.
(C) De Morgan's law for two sets. TRUE.
(D) Both sides are exactly the elements in precisely one of A and B. TRUE.
solution.misconception: (B) is accepted because difference “looks” associative, as union and intersection are. It is not: the order of subtraction matters, and the right-hand side removes less than the left.
solution.faster: For any claimed set identity, test one small case such as A = {1, 2}, B = {2}, C = {2} before doing algebra.
solution.takeaway: Difference is not associative; De Morgan and the symmetric-difference identity are the reliable rewrites.

questions.question: For finite sets A, B, C, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: |A ∪ B ∪ C| ≥ |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |B ∩ C| − |A ∩ C|

solution.concept: Monotonicity gives the first two bounds; the third-set inequality follows from the exact three-set formula by dropping the non-negative triple term.
steps: (A) A ⊆ A ∪ B and B ⊆ A ∪ B, so the union is at least as large as each part. TRUE.
(B) A ∩ B ⊆ A and A ∩ B ⊆ B. TRUE.
(C) Take |A| = 3, |B| = 5 disjoint; |A − B| = 3 but 3 − 5 = −2. FALSE.
(D) The exact identity has + |A ∩ B ∩ C| at the end; dropping a non-negative term can only lower the right side, so the inequality holds. TRUE.
solution.misconception: (C) is believed because “difference” suggests subtraction of sizes. The correct identity is |A − B| = |A| − |A ∩ B|, and |A| − |B| can even be negative.
solution.faster: Check (C) on disjoint sets, where it is most obviously wrong; that settles it without any algebra.
solution.takeaway: Sizes are monotone under ⊆, and the three-set formula becomes an inequality when the last term is dropped.

questions.question: Which of the following claims about products, partitions and equivalence relations are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: (A × B) ∪ (C × D) = (A ∪ C) × (B ∪ D) for all sets A, B, C, D.
For non-empty sets A and B, A × B = B × A if and only if A = B.
Every partition of a set A determines an equivalence relation on A.
The number of partitions of a 5-element set is 52.

solution.concept: Products are not distributive over unions in the way it looks; a partition and an equivalence relation are two views of the same data; the Bell numbers begin 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52.
steps: (A) Take A = {1}, B = {2}, C = {2}, D = {1}. Left side is {(1,2), (2,1)}, right side is {1,2} × {1,2}, which is larger. FALSE.
(B) If A × B = B × A then the sets of first coordinates agree, so A = B; the converse is immediate. TRUE.
(C) Declare x ~ y exactly when x and y lie in the same block; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity follow at once. TRUE.
solution.misconception: (A) looks like distributivity and is often accepted. A union of two products is much smaller than the product of the two unions; the two sides coincide only in degenerate cases.
solution.faster: For (A), test single-element sets with the coordinates crossed, as above; one counterexample settles it.
solution.takeaway: A partition and an equivalence relation are the same object seen twice; products of unions are not unions of products.

questions.question:
Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. How many ordered pairs of subsets (X, Y) satisfy X ⊆ Y ⊆ A, |X| = 2 and |Y| = 4?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Build the pair in two stages: choose the larger set Y first, then choose X from inside it. The constraint X ⊆ Y then holds automatically.
steps: Choose Y ⊆ A with |Y| = 4: C(5, 4) = 5 choices.
For a fixed Y, choose X ⊆ Y with |X| = 2: C(4, 2) = 6 choices.
The stages are independent, so the total is 5 · 6 = 30.
solution.misconception: Trying to count X first makes the condition X ⊆ Y awkward. Building the pair from the outside in is what keeps the count simple.
solution.faster: A chain of sizes is always counted outermost first: choose the largest set, then each smaller set inside it.
solution.takeaway: Order the nesting X ⊆ Y ⊆ A from the top down and multiply the binomial coefficients.

questions.question:
A finite set A satisfies |P(P(A))| = 256. What is |A|?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Iterating the power set raises 2 to the power repeatedly: |P(P(A))| = 2^{2^{|A|}}.
steps: Let |A| = n. Then |P(A)| = 2ⁿ and |P(P(A))| = 2^{2ⁿ}.
Set 2^{2ⁿ} = 256 = 2⁸.
So 2ⁿ = 8, giving n = 3.
solution.misconception: Halving 256 twice (256 → 128 → 64) instead of taking logarithms twice. The nesting is exponential in both layers, so 256 = 2^8 forces the inner power set to have size 8, not 128.
solution.faster: Write 256 as a power of 2, then solve the outer exponent as a power of 2 again: 256 = 2⁸ and 8 = 2³.
solution.takeaway: Each power set doubles the exponent: |P^k(A)| = 2↑↑k applied to n.

questions.question:
Let |A| = 18, |B| = 14 and |A ∩ B| = 5. How many elements lie in (A − B) ∪ (B − A)?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The set (A − B) ∪ (B − A) is the symmetric difference: the elements in exactly one of the two sets, so count each side separately and add.
steps: |A − B| = |A| − |A ∩ B| = 18 − 5 = 13.
|B − A| = |B| − |A ∩ B| = 14 − 5 = 9.
The two parts are disjoint, so the union has 13 + 9 = 22 elements.
solution.misconception: Computing |A| + |B| = 32 and forgetting to remove the overlap twice. Symmetric difference excludes the shared part entirely.
solution.faster: Symmetric difference count = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B| = 18 + 14 − 10 = 22.
solution.takeaway: Exactly-one-of-two counts as |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|.

questions.question:
In a survey of 100 people, 60 read newspaper A, 50 read B, 40 read C, 25 read A and B, 20 read B and C, 15 read A and C, and 10 read all three. How many read exactly one newspaper?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Exactly one = (sum of the three sizes) − 2·(sum of the three pairwise intersections) + 3·(triple intersection). Each person reading k papers must be counted exactly once.
steps: Sum of singles: 60 + 50 + 40 = 150.
Sum of pairwise intersections: 25 + 20 + 15 = 60.
Triple intersection: 10.
Exactly one = 150 − 2·60 + 3·10 = 150 − 120 + 30 = 60.
solution.misconception: Using 150 − 60 + 10 = 100, which is the union (and here also the whole population). Exactly-one needs the coefficients 1, −2, +3, not 1, −1, +1.
solution.faster: Compute the union first (150 − 60 + 10 = 100), then sanity-check your exactly-one figure against it — exactly one must be smaller than the union unless nobody reads two papers.
solution.takeaway: Exactly-one coefficients are 1, −2, +3; the union's are 1, −1, +1.

questions.question:
How many partitions does the set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The total number of partitions of an n-element set is the Bell number B(n), the sum of the Stirling numbers of the second kind over all block counts.
steps: Split by the number of blocks k: S(5,1) = 1, S(5,2) = 15, S(5,3) = 25, S(5,4) = 10, S(5,5) = 1.
Add: 1 + 15 + 25 + 10 + 1 = 52.
solution.misconception: Counting only the “interesting” partitions, or reporting S(5,2) = 15. The Bell number sums every possible number of blocks, including the one-block and five-block partitions.
solution.faster: Recall the Bell ladder 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; the fifth entry is the answer.
solution.takeaway: Bell numbers: 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203 — worth memorising to B(6).

questions.question: Let A = {a, b, c} and R = {(a,a), (b,b), (c,c), (a,b), (b,a)}. Which statement about R is TRUE?
options: R is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive.
R is an equivalence relation with exactly two equivalence classes.
R is a partial order on A.

solution.concept: An equivalence relation is exactly a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; its classes are the blocks it cuts the set into.
steps: Reflexive: (a,a), (b,b), (c,c) are all present.
Symmetric: the only off-diagonal pairs are (a,b) and (b,a), which come as a pair.
Transitive: the only compositions to check are (a,b) ∘ (b,a) = (a,a) and (b,a) ∘ (a,b) = (b,b), and both are in R.
So R is an equivalence relation. Its classes are {a, b} and {c} — exactly two.
why_wrong: (A) fails: the relation is transitive, as the two compositions above show.
(C) fails: (a,b) and (b,a) are both in R with a ≠ b, which is precisely what antisymmetry forbids.
(D) fails for the same reason: a partial order must be antisymmetric, and R is not.
solution.misconception: Students check transitivity only on pairs of the form (x,y), (y,z) that are both off-diagonal, and miss the compositions that involve a reversed pair.
solution.faster: A relation that is symmetric and antisymmetric can only contain diagonal pairs. Since this one has an off-diagonal pair, it cannot be antisymmetric — which kills (C) and (D) at once.
solution.takeaway: Symmetric and antisymmetric are not opposites; a relation can be both, but only if it contains no off-diagonal pair at all.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,4)}. Let R⁺ be the transitive closure of R. How many ordered pairs does the symmetric closure of R⁺ contain?

solution.concept: The transitive closure adds every pair (a,b) for which a path of length ≥ 1 runs from a to b; the symmetric closure then adds the reverse of every pair.
steps: Paths of length 1: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4).
Paths of length 2: (1,3), (2,4).
Paths of length 3: (1,4).
So R⁺ has 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs.
No pair in R⁺ has the form (x,x), so the symmetric closure adds exactly one new pair per pair: 6 + 6 = 12.
why_wrong: (A) 6 is |R⁺| itself; the reverses are forgotten.
(B) 10 is |R⁺| plus four reverses, which happens if the length-3 path (1,4) is missed.
(D) 16 is |A × A|, which would need the closure to be the universal relation.
solution.misconception: Two closures are routinely mixed up: the reflexive closure adds the diagonal pairs (x,x) (10 pairs here), while the symmetric closure adds the reverses (12 pairs here).
solution.faster: A chain of n links gives n(n+1)/2 ordered pairs in its transitive closure; here 4·3/2 = 6, then double it.
solution.takeaway: Count the closure level by level (path length 1, 2, 3, …) before applying the second closure.

questions.question: How many relations on a three-element set are both symmetric and antisymmetric?

solution.concept: Symmetry forces (a,b) and (b,a) to travel together; antisymmetry forbids them from both being present when a ≠ b. Together they force every off-diagonal pair out.
steps: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Take any a ≠ b with (a,b) ∈ R.
Symmetry gives (b,a) ∈ R; antisymmetry then forces a = b, a contradiction.
Hence R ⊆ {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)}.
Every subset of the three diagonal pairs is symmetric (no off-diagonal pair exists) and antisymmetric, so all 2³ = 8 subsets qualify.
why_wrong: (B) 16 = 2⁴ counts a relation on a two-element set, or treats one off-diagonal pair as free.
(C) 27 = 3³ is the number of antisymmetric relations on a three-element set on its own.
(D) 64 = 2⁶ is the number of symmetric relations on a three-element set on its own.
solution.misconception: The pair of adjectives is read as "symmetric or antisymmetric". The question asks for both, and the two conditions together are far more restrictive than either alone.
solution.faster: Symmetric ∧ antisymmetric ⟹ R ⊆ I_A, so the answer is always 2ⁿ for an n-element set.
solution.takeaway: Two extreme properties can intersect in a very small family — reason from the definitions rather than from counts of each separately.

questions.question: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} define aRb exactly when a ≡ b (mod 3). How many equivalence classes does R have?

solution.concept: Congruence modulo m is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the residue classes 0, 1, …, m−1.
steps: Residues of A modulo 3: 1 ≡ 4 ≡ 1, 2 ≡ 5 ≡ 2, 3 ≡ 6 ≡ 0.
The classes are {1, 4}, {2, 5} and {3, 6}.
There are three of them, indexed by the residues 0, 1, 2.
why_wrong: (A) 2 would be the answer for modulus 2.
(C) 4 counts the elements of the class {1, 4} as separate classes.
(D) 6 is |A|, the count for the identity relation.
solution.misconception: Students count the number of distinct residues present among the elements (0, 1, 2 — three) but then sometimes report the modulus range 0…2 as four values, or forget that residue 0 occurs (at 3 and 6).
solution.faster: The number of classes of congruence mod m on {1, …, n} is min(m, n) when the set is long enough to hit every residue; here 3.
solution.takeaway: Modulo m always yields exactly m classes on a set that covers all residues.

questions.question: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} define aRb exactly when |a − b| ≤ 2. Which defining property of an equivalence relation does R fail?
options: None — R is an equivalence relation

solution.concept: An equivalence relation must satisfy all three of reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity; a single counterexample to any one of them is enough to disqualify it.
steps: Reflexive: |a − a| = 0 ≤ 2 for every a, so (a,a) ∈ R.
Symmetric: |a − b| = |b − a|, so the condition is unchanged on swapping.
Transitive: take a = 1, b = 2, c = 4. Then |1 − 2| = 1 ≤ 2 and |2 − 4| = 2 ≤ 2, but |1 − 4| = 3 > 2, so (1,4) ∉ R.
Transitivity therefore fails.
why_wrong: (A) is wrong: distance 0 always satisfies ≤ 2.
(B) is wrong: absolute value is unchanged by reversing the order.
(D) is wrong because of the explicit counterexample 1R2, 2R4 yet 1R̸4.
solution.misconception: A "close enough" relation feels like it should be transitive. Distances add up, so a tolerance relation is almost never transitive — it fails exactly when the two hops together exceed the tolerance.
solution.faster: Any relation of the form |a − b| ≤ k with k ≥ 1 is reflexive and symmetric but transitive only when k = 0.
solution.takeaway: Tolerance relations are the standard counterexample that reflexive + symmetric does not give an equivalence relation.

questions.question: How many equivalence relations on A = {1, 2, 3, 4} place 1 and 2 in the same class?

solution.concept: Equivalence relations on A correspond one-to-one with partitions of A; requiring 1 and 2 to share a class means gluing them into one block before partitioning.
steps: Fuse 1 and 2 into a single block B = {1, 2}.
The remaining partition problem is over the three objects B, 3, 4.
The number of partitions of a three-element set is the Bell number B(3) = 5.
So there are 5 such equivalence relations.
why_wrong: (A) 4 = B(3) − 1, dropping one of the five partitions.
(C) 7 counts the partitions of {1,2,3} plus the ones of {1,2,3,4} that keep 1 and 2 apart, which the question excludes.
(D) 8 is 2³, treating each of the three objects as independently in or out of the block containing 1 and 2 — which double counts.
solution.misconception: Students try to count partitions of four elements and then filter, which is error-prone. Contracting the forced pair first turns the problem into a smaller standard one.
solution.faster: Number of partitions of n elements in which a fixed k-set stays together = B(n − k + 1); here B(3) = 5.
solution.takeaway: "Two elements must be together" is a contraction — reduce the ground set by one and use the Bell number.

questions.question: Which of the following relations on {1, 2, 3} is a partial order?

solution.concept: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; all three must hold simultaneously.
steps: (A) is reflexive and transitive but not antisymmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) are both present with 1 ≠ 2.
(B) is reflexive and antisymmetric but not transitive: (1,2) and (2,3) are present while (1,3) is not.
(C) is the usual order ≤ on {1,2,3}: reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive because 1 < 2 < 3 gives 1 < 3.
(D) is transitive and antisymmetric but not reflexive — it is a strict order, and it is missing (1,1), (2,2), (3,3).
why_wrong: (A) fails antisymmetry — it contains a 2-cycle.
(B) fails transitivity — it is missing the short-circuit pair (1,3).
(D) fails reflexivity — no diagonal pairs at all.
solution.misconception: Reflexivity is the property most often skipped when students scan a list of pairs; and strict orders (like <) are routinely mistaken for partial orders.
solution.faster: Check the three properties in the order reflexivity → antisymmetry → transitivity; the first list that fails one is out, and you rarely need to check all three for every option.
solution.takeaway: A partial order is ≤-like, not <-like: the diagonal is mandatory.

questions.question: In the divisibility poset on {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, how many edges does the Hasse diagram have?

solution.concept: A Hasse diagram draws one edge for each covering relation: a covers b when b < a and no element lies strictly between them.
steps: List the covering pairs. 1 is covered by exactly the atoms 2 and 3.
Above 2: 4 and 6 cover it (both quotients are prime).
Above 3: only 6 covers it.
Above 4: 12 covers it; above 6: 12 covers it.
why_wrong: (A) 6 is what you get by dropping the edge 2–6 and forgetting that 6 covers 2.
(C) 8 usually comes from drawing 3–12 (3 divides 12, but 6 lies in between, so 12 does not cover 3).
(D) 9 usually comes from drawing both 3–12 and 2–12.
solution.misconception: Every divisor pair is drawn as an edge. In a Hasse diagram divisibility alone is not enough — the pair must be a covering pair.
solution.faster: In a divisor-closed set, a covers b exactly when a / b is prime. Count the pairs (a, b) with a/b prime: 12/6, 12/4, 6/3, 6/2, 4/2, 3/1, 2/1 — seven.
solution.takeaway: Hasse edge = covering pair = quotient is prime (inside a divisor-closed set).

questions.question: In the poset ({1, 2, …, 30}, ∣) ordered by divisibility, what is the size of a largest antichain?

solution.concept: An antichain is a set of pairwise incomparable elements. If the poset can be split into c chains, every antichain meets each chain at most once, so it has at most c elements.
steps: Write every n ≤ 30 uniquely as n = 2^k · m with m odd.
Numbers sharing the same odd part m form a chain m, 2m, 4m, …, since each divides the next.
The odd parts that occur are the 15 odd numbers 1, 3, 5, …, 29, so the poset splits into 15 chains.
Hence every antichain has at most 15 elements.
The interval {16, 17, …, 30} is an antichain: for a < b in it, 2a ≥ 32 > 30, so a ∤ b. It has 15 elements.
why_wrong: (A) 10 comes from using only the 10 primes up to 30, which is a different (and smaller) antichain question.
(C) 16 is an off-by-one on the interval {15, …, 30} — but 15 divides 30, so that interval is not an antichain.
(D) 30 is the whole set, which is far from an antichain.
solution.misconception: The upper half {16, …, 30} looks obviously incomparable by size, but students forget to check divisibility inside it and often include 15 as well.
solution.faster: For {1, …, 2n} the largest antichain under divisibility always has n elements; here n = 15.
solution.takeaway: Chain decomposition gives the upper bound, an explicit interval gives the lower bound — matching them proves the maximum.

questions.question: Which of the following posets is NOT a lattice?
options: (ℤ⁺, ∣) — the positive integers under divisibility
The poset with elements {0, a, b} where 0 < a, 0 < b and a, b are incomparable

solution.concept: A lattice is a poset in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound inside the poset.
steps: (A): A ∨ B = A ∪ B and A ∧ B = A ∩ B — always a lattice.
(B): a ∨ b = lcm(a,b) and a ∧ b = gcd(a,b) — always a lattice.
(C): the upper bounds of a and b form the empty set, so no least upper bound exists. Not a lattice.
(D): the set is divisor-closed, so every pair has both a join and a meet inside it: 2 ∨ 3 = lcm(2,3) = 6, 6 ∨ 12 = 12, 2 ∧ 12 = gcd(2,12) = 2, 3 ∧ 12 = 3. A lattice.
why_wrong: (A) is the Boolean lattice 2^S, the archetypal lattice.
(B) is the divisibility lattice of the positive integers, with lcm as join.
(D) is the divisor lattice of 12 restricted to a divisor-closed set, hence closed under both operations.
solution.misconception: "Incomparable" is confused with "no join". Two incomparable elements can still have a join — the failure in (C) is that they have no common upper bound at all.
solution.faster: Look for two elements with no common upper bound, or with two minimal common upper bounds. Either defect immediately disqualifies a lattice.
solution.takeaway: A lattice needs joins and meets for every pair, not just for comparable pairs.

questions.question: For a positive integer n, let D(n) be the lattice of positive divisors of n under divisibility. D(n) is a Boolean lattice exactly when
options: n is a product of distinct primes
n is a power of a prime

solution.concept: If n = p₁^{e₁} … p_k^{e_k}, then D(n) is isomorphic to the product of chains C_{e₁+1} × … × C_{e_k+1}. A Boolean lattice is a product of copies of the two-element chain.
steps: Each divisor corresponds to a tuple of exponents (a₁, …, a_k) with 0 ≤ aᵢ ≤ eᵢ, ordered coordinatewise.
That is a product of chains of lengths eᵢ + 1.
A product of chains is Boolean only when every factor is the two-element chain, i.e. every eᵢ = 1.
So D(n) ≅ 2^k exactly when n is squarefree, a product of distinct primes.
solution.final: Option (B) — n is a product of distinct primes.
why_wrong: (A) a prime gives D(p) ≅ 2¹, which is Boolean, but the condition must characterise all cases; n = 12 is neither prime nor Boolean, so (A) is too narrow.
(C) D(p³) is a chain of four elements — it has a chain of length 3, which no Boolean lattice has.
(D) n = 12 = 2² · 3 is even and D(12) is not Boolean.
solution.misconception: Prime powers feel "simple" and are assumed to give Boolean lattices; in fact they give chains, the opposite extreme.
solution.faster: Count atoms: D(n) is Boolean iff it has k atoms and exactly 2^k elements. For n = 12 there are 2 atoms but 6 elements ≠ 4.
solution.takeaway: Boolean divisor lattice ⟺ squarefree n; prime power ⟺ chain.

questions.question: Let R = {(1,2), (2,3)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. What is the composite relation R ∘ R?

solution.concept: (a,c) ∈ S ∘ R exactly when some b satisfies (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S — a two-step walk.
steps: Start at 1: the only pair out of 1 is (1,2), so continue from 2. The only pair out of 2 is (2,3), giving (1,3).
Start at 2: leads to 3, and nothing leaves 3, so no pair.
Start at 3: nothing leaves 3, so no pair.
Hence R ∘ R = {(1,3)}.
why_wrong: (A) is R itself, not the composite.
(C) is the transitive closure R⁺, which unions R with R².
(D) would need no two-step walk to exist, but 1 → 2 → 3 is one.
solution.misconception: R² is read as "the transitive closure" or as "square each element". Composition is path concatenation of exactly two steps.
solution.faster: Build a 3×3 boolean matrix for R and square it; the ones in R² are the two-step walks.
solution.takeaway: R² = two-step walks only; R⁺ = walks of every positive length.

questions.question: Let R = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,4)} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. How many ordered pairs are in the transitive closure R⁺?

solution.concept: The transitive closure contains (a,b) exactly when a walk of positive length runs from a to b.
steps: The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) form a 2-cycle, so from 1 you can reach 2, and from 2 you can reach 1.
Composing the cycle with itself gives (1,1) and (2,2), which must be added.
The pair (3,4) is isolated: nothing leaves 4 and nothing enters 3, so it generates no new pair.
why_wrong: (A) 4 keeps only R and forgets that a cycle forces its diagonal pairs into the closure.
(C) 6 would need an extra pair such as (3,3) or (4,4), which requires a walk, not just an element.
(D) 7 would need both diagonals of the isolated pair as well.
solution.misconception: The transitive closure is assumed to be the reflexive-transitive closure. Here the diagonal pairs come from the cycle, not from reflexivity — (3,3) and (4,4) are correctly absent.
solution.faster: Any strongly connected component of size s ≥ 2 contributes all s² pairs to R⁺; here 2² + 1 = 5.
solution.takeaway: Cycles generate diagonal pairs inside the closure; isolated edges generate nothing extra.

questions.question: How many relations are there on a set with three elements?

solution.concept: A relation on A is any subset of A × A, so the count is 2^{|A|²}.
steps: With |A| = 3, the product set has 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs.
Each of those nine pairs is independently either in or out of the relation.
So the number of relations is 2⁹ = 512.
why_wrong: (A) 64 = 2⁶ counts relations on a three-element set that are forced to be symmetric (6 free choices), or relations on a set of size 2.45 — not a valid interpretation.
(B) 256 = 2⁸ comes from using n² − 1 free pairs, an off-by-one.
(D) 729 = 3⁶ is the number of functions from a 6-element set, not of relations.
solution.misconception: The exponent is |A × A| = n², not n. Students who write 2³ = 8 are counting subsets of A instead.
solution.faster: Memorise the ladder: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 2, 16, 512, 65536 relations.
solution.takeaway: Relations on an n-element set: 2^{n²}.

questions.question: How many reflexive relations are there on a set with four elements?

solution.concept: Reflexivity forces the n diagonal pairs into the relation; every other pair stays free, so the count is 2^{n² − n}.
steps: There are 4² = 16 ordered pairs in total.
The four diagonal pairs (a,a) must be included — no freedom there.
The remaining 16 − 4 = 12 pairs are free.
So the number of reflexive relations is 2¹² = 4096.
why_wrong: (A) 1024 = 2¹⁰ subtracts the wrong number of forced pairs.
(B) 2048 = 2¹¹ is the count for a set of size 4 where only three pairs are forced.
(D) 65536 = 2¹⁶ counts all relations, ignoring reflexivity entirely.
solution.misconception: Students subtract n from n² but then compute 2^n instead of 2^{n²−n}; or they forget that the diagonal is forced *in*, not just removed from the count.
solution.faster: Reflexive: 2^{n(n−1)}. Here 2^{12} = 4096.
solution.takeaway: Reflexive relations: 2^{n(n−1)}; irreflexive: the same count; symmetric: 2^{n(n+1)/2}.

questions.question: For relations on a finite set A, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric is contained in the identity relation.
If R is symmetric then R⁻¹ = R.
If R is reflexive and symmetric then R is transitive.
If R is an equivalence relation then so is A × A − R.

solution.concept: Each option is settled by applying the definition directly or by exhibiting one small counterexample.
steps: (A): if (a,b) ∈ R with a ≠ b, symmetry gives (b,a) ∈ R and antisymmetry then forces a = b — contradiction. So only diagonal pairs can occur. TRUE.
(B): R⁻¹ = {(b,a) : (a,b) ∈ R}, and symmetry says (a,b) ∈ R ⇔ (b,a) ∈ R, so the two sets coincide. TRUE.
(C): on A = {1,2,3} take R = I_A ∪ {(1,2), (2,1), (2,3), (3,2)}. It is reflexive and symmetric, yet (1,2), (2,3) ∈ R while (1,3) ∉ R. FALSE.
(D): with |A| ≥ 2, A × A − R omits every diagonal pair, so it is not reflexive and hence not an equivalence relation. FALSE.
why_wrong: (C) fails because reflexivity plus symmetry says nothing about paths of length two.
(D) fails because an equivalence relation must contain I_A, and the complement of a set containing I_A cannot contain I_A.
solution.misconception: The complement of a nice relation is assumed to be nice. Complementing destroys reflexivity first, which kills (D) immediately.
solution.faster: Check (D) by reflexivity alone — the fastest possible kill — then look for the standard "reflexive + symmetric but not transitive" counterexample for (C).
solution.takeaway: Symmetric ∧ antisymmetric forces containment in I_A; the complement of a reflexive relation is never reflexive.

questions.question: Let R be an equivalence relation on a non-empty set A, and let [a] denote the equivalence class of a. Which of the following are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every element of A lies in exactly one equivalence class.
aRb if and only if [a] = [b].
Any two distinct equivalence classes are disjoint.
R has exactly |A| equivalence classes.

solution.concept: The equivalence classes of R form a partition of A: non-empty, pairwise disjoint, and covering A.
steps: (A): a ∈ [a] by reflexivity, so every element is in at least one class; if a ∈ [b] ∩ [c] then bRa and aRc, so bRc and [b] = [c] — at most one class. TRUE.
(B): if aRb and x ∈ [a], then xRa and aRb give xRb, so [a] ⊆ [b]; symmetrically [b] ⊆ [a]. Conversely [a] = [b] with a ∈ [a] gives a ∈ [b], i.e. aRb. TRUE.
(C): if c ∈ [a] ∩ [b] then [c] = [a] and [c] = [b] by (B), so [a] = [b]. TRUE.
(D): the universal relation on A has one class, not |A|; the identity relation has |A|. FALSE.
why_wrong: (D) fails: the number of classes ranges from 1 to |A| depending on R.
solution.misconception: The count of classes is confused with the size of the set. |A| classes is the maximum, attained only by the identity relation.
solution.faster: Everything about equivalence classes follows from "classes = blocks of a partition"; three of the four options are just restatements of that.
solution.takeaway: Equivalence relation ⟷ partition: the classes are the blocks, and there is no fourth option.

questions.question: Consider the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}. Which of the following are covering relations in this poset? (Select all that apply.)

solution.concept: a covers b when b ∣ a, b ≠ a, and no element of the poset lies strictly between them.
steps: (A) 4 ∣ 8 and the only element of P strictly between them would divide 8 and be divisible by 4 — none exists. TRUE.
(B) 2 ∣ 6 and the only candidate strictly between is 3, which does not divide 6 within a chain from 2… in fact no element of P lies strictly between 2 and 6 (3 is not above 2). TRUE.
(C) 6 ∣ 12 and no element of P lies strictly between 6 and 12 (the divisors of 12 above 6 are only 12). TRUE.
(D) 6 ∣ 24, but 12 ∈ P satisfies 6 ∣ 12 ∣ 24, so 12 lies strictly between them. FALSE.
why_wrong: (D) fails because the intermediate element 12 is present in P: 6 ∣ 12 ∣ 24, so 24 does not cover 6. (Note that 24 does cover 8, since no element of P lies between 8 and 24.)
solution.misconception: Divisibility is taken as covering. Covering is a statement about the *specific* poset: 24 covers 8 here precisely because 12 is not a multiple of 8, while 24 fails to cover 6 because 12 is a multiple of 6.
solution.faster: When the poset is divisor-closed (as P is), a covers b exactly when a/b is prime. Here 8/4 = 2, 6/2 = 3, 12/6 = 2 are prime, while 24/6 = 4 is not.
solution.takeaway: In a divisor-closed poset, covering ⟺ the quotient is prime; the moment an intermediate element is present, the quotient is composite.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about lattices are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every finite lattice has a least element and a greatest element.
In a distributive lattice an element has at most one complement.
In every bounded lattice every element has a complement.

solution.concept: A finite lattice is bounded because the join and meet of all elements exist; distributivity is an extra axiom, and complementedness is another.
steps: (A): in a finite lattice the join of all elements is the greatest element and the meet of all elements is the least element. TRUE.
(B): if b and c are both complements of a, then b = b ∧ 1 = b ∧ (a ∨ c) = (b ∧ a) ∨ (b ∧ c) = 0 ∨ (b ∧ c) = b ∧ c, and symmetrically c = b ∧ c, so b = c. TRUE.
(C): the diamond M₃ and the pentagon N₅ are lattices that are not distributive. FALSE.
(D): in N₅ the middle element has no complement. FALSE.
why_wrong: (C) fails on the two classic non-distributive lattices M₃ and N₅.
(D) fails because boundedness guarantees only that 0 and 1 exist, not that every element has a complement.
solution.misconception: Bounded is read as complemented. A bounded lattice may have elements with no complement at all, and in a non-distributive lattice an element may have several.
solution.faster: Distributive + bounded + complemented = Boolean; each adjective is independent, and (C) and (D) each assert that one of them is automatic.
solution.takeaway: Distributivity and complementedness are independent extras; only distributivity makes complements unique.

questions.question: Let R and S be relations on a set A. Which of the following identities hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: R ∘ R⁻¹ is the identity relation on A

solution.concept: Inversion commutes with union, intersection and difference because it only swaps the two coordinates of each pair; composition reverses the order of the factors.
steps: (A): (a,b) ∈ (R ∪ S)⁻¹ ⇔ (b,a) ∈ R ∪ S ⇔ (b,a) ∈ R or (b,a) ∈ S ⇔ (a,b) ∈ R⁻¹ ∪ S⁻¹. TRUE.
(B): the same argument with "or" replaced by "and". TRUE.
(C): (a,c) ∈ (S ∘ R)⁻¹ ⇔ (c,a) ∈ S ∘ R ⇔ ∃b, (c,b) ∈ S, (b,a) ∈ R ⇔ ∃b, (b,c) ∈ S⁻¹, (a,b) ∈ R⁻¹ ⇔ (a,c) ∈ R⁻¹ ∘ S⁻¹. TRUE.
(D): R ∘ R⁻¹ = {(a,a) : ∃b, (a,b) ∈ R}. If some element of A has no R-image, its diagonal pair is missing, so the relation is only a subset of I_A. FALSE.
why_wrong: (D) fails whenever R is not total, e.g. R = {(1,2)} on A = {1,2} gives only (1,1).
solution.misconception: The inverse of a composite is written in the same order. It must be reversed: (S ∘ R)⁻¹ = R⁻¹ ∘ S⁻¹, like inverting a product of matrices.
solution.faster: For composition, read right-to-left in both the original and the inverse; for union and intersection the inverse distributes freely.
solution.takeaway: R ∘ R⁻¹ is the identity restricted to the domain of R, not the identity on A.

questions.question:
How many symmetric relations are there on a set with three elements?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A symmetric relation is determined independently on the diagonal pairs and on each unordered pair {a, b}: for off-diagonal pairs symmetry forces both (a,b) and (b,a) to be in, or both to be out.
steps: There are 3 diagonal pairs, each free: 2³ choices.
There are C(3,2) = 3 unordered off-diagonal pairs; symmetry makes each an all-or-nothing choice: 2³ choices.
Multiply: 2³ · 2³ = 2⁶ = 64.
solution.misconception: Counting 2⁹ = 512 by treating all nine pairs as independent — symmetry couples the pairs (a,b) and (b,a).
solution.faster: Symmetric relations on n elements: 2^{n(n+1)/2}; here 2⁶ = 64.
solution.takeaway: Symmetric: 2^{n(n+1)/2}. Antisymmetric: 2ⁿ · 3^{n(n−1)/2}.

questions.question:
How many antisymmetric relations are there on a set with two elements?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Antisymmetry only constrains pairs of the form (a,b) and (b,a) with a ≠ b: they may not both be present.
steps: Let A = {1, 2}. The two diagonal pairs are unconstrained: 2² = 4 choices.
For the pair {1, 2} there are three legal states: include neither, include only (1,2), include only (2,1).
Multiply: 4 × 3 = 12.
solution.misconception: Counting 2⁴ = 16 by treating all four pairs as free — the state "both (1,2) and (2,1)" is exactly what antisymmetry forbids.
solution.faster: Antisymmetric relations on n elements: 2ⁿ · 3^{n(n−1)/2}; here 4 × 3 = 12.
solution.takeaway: Antisymmetry: each unordered off-diagonal pair has 3 legal states, each diagonal pair 2.

questions.question:
In the divisor lattice D(72) — the positive divisors of 72 ordered by divisibility — how many elements have a complement?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: In a bounded lattice, e is a complement of d when d ∧ e = 1 and d ∨ e = 72, i.e. gcd(d,e) = 1 and lcm(d,e) = 72.
steps: Write 72 = 2³ · 3². A divisor is d = 2^i 3^j with 0 ≤ i ≤ 3, 0 ≤ j ≤ 2.
The two conditions together force d · e = 72, so e = 72/d is the only candidate.
Then gcd(d, 72/d) = 1 requires d to take each prime's full exponent or none: i ∈ {0, 3} and j ∈ {0, 2}.
That gives 2 × 2 = 4 divisors: 1, 8, 9, 72, with complements 72, 9, 8, 1.
solution.misconception: D(72) is distributive and bounded, so students assume every element has a complement. Distributive + bounded is not complemented — the standard counterexample is exactly this kind of divisor lattice.
solution.faster: Such divisors are the unitary divisors of n: 2^k of them, where k is the number of distinct primes. Here 2² = 4.
solution.takeaway: In D(n), exactly 2^{ω(n)} elements have complements, where ω(n) is the number of distinct primes dividing n.

questions.question:
Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and let R be the smallest equivalence relation on A containing {(1,2), (3,4)}. How many equivalence classes does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The smallest equivalence relation containing a set of pairs is obtained by taking the symmetric, transitive, reflexive closure — equivalently, by merging the elements that the given pairs force together.
steps: The pair (1,2) forces 1 and 2 into one class; the pair (3,4) forces 3 and 4 into another.
Element 5 is in no given pair, so it stays alone.
No given pair links the block {1,2} to the block {3,4} or to 5, so nothing further merges.
Classes: {1,2}, {3,4}, {5} — three in total.
solution.misconception: Students apply transitivity across the two given pairs, as if 2 were related to 3. It is not: the pairs (1,2) and (3,4) share no element.
solution.faster: Count the connected components of the graph whose edges are the given pairs, then add the isolated vertices.
solution.takeaway: Smallest equivalence relation = connected components of the relation graph; each component is one class.

questions.question:
On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (4,5)}. How many ordered pairs are in the transitive closure R⁺?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The transitive closure contains (a,b) exactly when a walk of positive length runs from a to b.
steps: Elements 1, 2, 3 form a directed cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 1, so every element of the cycle reaches every element of the cycle.
That contributes 3² = 9 pairs.
The pair (4,5) is isolated from the cycle and adds exactly one pair.
Total: 9 + 1 = 10.
solution.misconception: Students count only the cycle's own three pairs plus (4,5) and get 4, forgetting that a strongly connected component contributes all s² pairs.
solution.faster: A strongly connected component of size s contributes s² pairs to R⁺; add the pairs from all other components separately.
solution.takeaway: Collapse R into strongly connected components, then count Σ s² over the components.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)}. Which statement about R is TRUE?
options: R is reflexive and antisymmetric but not transitive.
R is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
R is an equivalence relation on A.

solution.concept: A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; transitivity constrains only the two-step paths that actually exist.
steps: Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) are all present.
Antisymmetric: the only off-diagonal pair is (1,2), and its reverse (2,1) is absent.
Transitive: the only two-step path is (1,2) followed by (2,2), whose shortcut (1,2) is present; every other chain is a self-loop on the diagonal.
So R is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive — a partial order in which 3 is incomparable with 1 and 2.
why_wrong: (A) fails because R is transitive, as the single chain above shows.
(C) fails because (1,2) ∈ R but (2,1) ∉ R.
(D) fails because an equivalence relation must be symmetric, and R is not.
solution.misconception: Students often assume that any off-diagonal pair destroys transitivity. Transitivity fails only when some two-step path has its shortcut missing.
solution.faster: List the two-step paths rather than the pairs: here exactly one exists, and its shortcut is already in the relation.
solution.takeaway: Transitivity is a statement about existing chains, not about how many pairs a relation contains.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and R = {(1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1), (2,3), (3,2)}. Which statement about R is TRUE?
options: R is symmetric but not transitive.
R is transitive but not symmetric.
R is an equivalence relation on A.

solution.concept: Symmetry asks only that every pair be accompanied by its reverse; transitivity additionally forces the diagonal pairs once two opposite off-diagonal pairs are present.
steps: Every one of the six off-diagonal pairs appears together with its reverse, so R is symmetric.
None of (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) lies in R, so R is not reflexive.
Both (1,2) and (2,1) are in R, so transitivity would force (1,1) — and it is absent.
Hence R is symmetric but not transitive.
why_wrong: (A) fails on reflexivity: no diagonal pair is present.
(C) fails because R is symmetric — all six off-diagonal pairs come in reverse pairs.
(D) fails twice over: an equivalence relation must be reflexive and transitive.
solution.misconception: Seeing all six off-diagonal pairs and concluding "the complete relation, hence an equivalence relation". The complete relation on A is A × A, which also contains the diagonal.
solution.faster: If a symmetric relation contains (a,b) and (b,a) with a ≠ b, transitivity forces (a,a) and (b,b). A missing diagonal is an instant transitivity failure.
solution.takeaway: A × A minus the diagonal is symmetric and irreflexive, and therefore never transitive when |A| ≥ 2.

questions.question: For a relation R on a set A, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If R is both symmetric and antisymmetric, then R ⊆ {(a,a) : a ∈ A}.
If R is irreflexive and transitive, then R ∩ R⁻¹ = ∅.

solution.concept: Antisymmetry forbids a pair and its reverse only when the two endpoints are distinct; asymmetry forbids a pair and its reverse outright, including a self-pair.
steps: (A) Suppose (a,b) ∈ R with a ≠ b. Symmetry gives (b,a) ∈ R, and antisymmetry then forces a = b — a contradiction. So R has no off-diagonal pair.
(B) Asymmetry says (a,b) ∈ R ⇒ (b,a) ∉ R. For a ≠ b that is exactly the antisymmetry condition, so asymmetric implies antisymmetric.
(C) fails: the identity relation I_A is antisymmetric, yet (a,a) is in it, so it is not asymmetric.
(D) If (a,b) and (b,a) were both in R with a ≠ b, transitivity would give (a,a), contradicting irreflexivity. So R and R⁻¹ share no pair.
why_wrong: (C) is the trap: antisymmetry permits diagonal pairs, asymmetry does not, so the implication runs the other way.
solution.misconception: "Antisymmetric" is often read as "no pair has its reverse", which is asymmetry. Antisymmetry only forbids off-diagonal reversals.
solution.faster: Order the notions by strength: asymmetric = antisymmetric + irreflexive. Anything asymmetric is automatically antisymmetric, never the reverse.
solution.takeaway: Antisymmetric allows (a,a); asymmetric does not. Irreflexive plus transitive always yields asymmetry.

questions.question: Let R be a relation on a finite set A that is irreflexive and transitive. Which of the following must be TRUE?

solution.concept: An irreflexive transitive relation is a strict partial order, and strictness rules out any pair occurring together with its reverse.
steps: Suppose both (a,b) and (b,a) lie in R.
Transitivity applied to those two pairs yields (a,a) ∈ R.
Irreflexivity forbids (a,a) ∈ R, so the supposition is impossible.
Therefore (b,a) ∉ R for every (a,b) ∈ R — that is, R is asymmetric. Option (B) holds.
The other options fail in general: on {1, 2, 3} the relation R = {(1,2)} is irreflexive and transitive, but it is neither symmetric nor reflexive, and R ∪ I_A is not symmetric either.
why_wrong: (A) fails for R = {(1,2)}: the reverse pair (2,1) is missing.
(C) fails because R ∪ I_A contains (1,2) but not (2,1).
(D) contradicts the stated irreflexivity of R.
solution.misconception: "Irreflexive and transitive" is often taken to mean "no cycles of any length", which is stronger than what is given. In fact it is exactly strictness.
solution.faster: Remember the one-line argument: a two-cycle plus transitivity manufactures a self-loop, so irreflexivity kills every two-cycle.
solution.takeaway: A strict partial order (irreflexive + transitive) is automatically asymmetric.

questions.question:
How many relations on the set A = {1, 2, 3} are symmetric and transitive but not reflexive?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A symmetric transitive relation is an equivalence relation on its own field, so counting them means choosing which elements are used and then partitioning them.
steps: If R is symmetric and transitive, its field F = {a : (a,b) ∈ R for some b} is closed: for a ∈ F symmetry gives (b,a) ∈ R and transitivity gives (a,a) ∈ R. So R restricted to F is an equivalence relation.
Such an R is therefore determined by a subset F ⊆ A and a partition of it.
Summing over all fields: 1 + 3·B₁ + 3·B₂ + B₃ = 1 + 3 + 6 + 5 = 15.
R is reflexive exactly when F = A, which accounts for the B₃ = 5 partitions of A.
Answer: 15 − 5 = 10.
solution.misconception: Counting only the five partitions of A and forgetting that the field may be a proper subset. That yields 0 instead of 10.
solution.faster: Symmetric and transitive relations on n elements number Σ C(n,k)·B(k); subtract B(n) for the reflexive ones.
solution.takeaway: Symmetry plus transitivity already forces reflexivity on the field, so the only freedom is which elements are used at all.

questions.question: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} define aRb exactly when a ≡ b (mod 4). How many equivalence classes does R have, and how large is the class containing 6?
options: 4 classes; the class of 6 has 2 elements.
4 classes; the class of 6 has 3 elements.
8 classes; the class of 6 has 1 element.
2 classes; the class of 6 has 4 elements.

solution.concept: Congruence modulo m is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the residue classes intersected with the given set.
steps: The residues of 1…8 modulo 4 are 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0.
Classes: {4, 8}, {1, 5}, {2, 6}, {3, 7} — four classes.
Since 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4), the class of 6 is {2, 6}, of size 2.
Answer: 4 classes, and the class of 6 has 2 elements.
why_wrong: (B) miscounts {2, 6} as three elements.
(C) treats congruence as equality, which would give eight singleton classes.
(D) confuses the number of classes with the size of a class.
solution.misconception: Assuming the number of classes always equals the modulus. That holds here because 1…8 hits all four residues, but it fails when the modulus exceeds the range of the set.
solution.faster: A class is the intersection of the set with one residue class; list the residues actually attained.
solution.takeaway: The number of classes is the number of residues attained, and classes may be singletons.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and let R be the smallest equivalence relation on A containing the pair (1,3). How many ordered pairs does R contain?

solution.concept: The smallest equivalence relation containing a set of pairs is the one induced by the partition generated by those pairs; its size is the sum of the squared class sizes.
steps: Symmetry forces (3,1), and reflexivity together with transitivity forces (1,1) and (3,3).
So 1 and 3 form one class {1, 3}, while 2 and 4 each form their own class.
Pairs: 2² = 4 from {1, 3}, plus 1 from {2} and 1 from {4}.
Total 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
why_wrong: (A) counts only the four diagonal pairs and drops both orders of the pair {1, 3}.
(C) adds the diagonal plus both orders of every pair, which would be the relation with two classes {1, 3} and {2, 4}.
(D) is A × A, the one-class relation, which also merges 2 and 4.
solution.misconception: Adding (3,1) alone and forgetting that reflexivity then contributes (1,1) and (3,3).
solution.faster: Contract each given pair into a block, keep everything else singleton, then compute Σ |C|² over the blocks.
solution.takeaway: An equivalence relation with classes C₁, …, C_k contains exactly Σ |C_i|² ordered pairs.

questions.question: Let A be a finite set with |A| = n ≥ 1. Which of the following statements about equivalence relations on A are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The number of equivalence relations on A equals the number of partitions of A.
An equivalence relation on A with exactly n classes must be the identity relation I_A.
Every equivalence relation on A contains at least n ordered pairs.
An equivalence relation on A with exactly one class contains exactly n ordered pairs.

solution.concept: Equivalence relations on A and partitions of A are two descriptions of the same object: the classes of the relation are the blocks of the partition.
steps: (A) is that bijection: send %s to its set of classes, and send a partition to the relation "lies in the same block".
(B) %s classes on %s elements force every class to be a singleton, so the relation is exactly the diagonal.
(C) Reflexivity alone contributes the n diagonal pairs, so |R| ≥ n.
(D) fails: one class means R = A × A, which has n² pairs, not n.
why_wrong: (D) is the trap: the coarsest equivalence relation is the largest one, not the smallest.
solution.misconception: Believing that a relation with few classes has few pairs. The number of pairs grows as the classes grow.
solution.faster: Always compute |R| = Σ |C|² over the classes: the discrete partition gives n and the one-block partition gives n².
solution.takeaway: Counting equivalence relations means counting partitions; the pair count is the sum of squared block sizes.

questions.question:
How many equivalence relations on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} have exactly three equivalence classes?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Equivalence relations on an n-element set with exactly k classes are counted by the Stirling number of the second kind S(n,k) — the number of partitions into k non-empty blocks.
steps: Use the recurrence S(5,3) = 3·S(4,3) + S(4,2): either the new element 5 joins one of the three existing blocks, or it opens a fourth block that must then be merged.
From the Stirling triangle, S(4,3) = 6 and S(4,2) = 7.
So S(5,3) = 3·6 + 7 = 25.
Cross-check with the closed form (3⁵ − 3·2⁵ + 3)/6 = (243 − 96 + 3)/6 = 150/6 = 25.
solution.misconception: Using C(5,3) = 10 — choosing which three elements are alone — and stopping there. That ignores whether the remaining two elements are together or separate.
solution.faster: Memorise the small Stirling triangle: 1 / 1 1 / 1 3 1 / 1 7 6 1 / 1 15 25 10 1.
solution.takeaway: Equivalence relations with exactly k classes = S(n,k).

questions.question: In the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 4, 8}, which element does 4 cover?

solution.concept: b covers a when a ∣ b, a ≠ b, and no third element of the poset lies strictly between them.
steps: The elements of P dividing 4 are 1 and 2.
Since 1 ∣ 2 ∣ 4, the element 1 lies strictly below 4 through 2, so 4 does not cover 1.
Nothing in P lies strictly between 2 and 4, so 4 covers 2.
Answer: 4 covers 2.
why_wrong: (A) 1 is below 2, so the cover relation skips it.
(C) 8 lies above 4; a cover must be above.
(D) is false, since 2 is covered by 4.
solution.misconception: Reading "covers" as "is divisible by", which would make 4 cover both 1 and 2.
solution.faster: In a divisor-closed set, b covers a exactly when b/a is prime. Here 4/2 = 2 is prime but 4/1 = 4 is not.
solution.takeaway: In divisibility posets a cover multiplies by exactly one prime factor.

questions.question: In the divisibility poset on {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30}, how many edges does the Hasse diagram have?

solution.concept: Hasse-diagram edges are the covering relations; in a divisor-closed set, b covers a exactly when b/a is prime.
steps: Group by the number of prime factors: 1 at level 0; 2, 3, 5 at level 1; 6, 10, 15 at level 2; 30 at level 3.
Level 0 to level 1: 2, 3, 5 covers 1 — three edges.
Level 1 to level 2: 6 covers 2 and 3; 10 covers 2 and 5; 15 covers 3 and 5 — six edges.
Level 2 to level 3: 30 covers 6, 10 and 15 — three edges.
Total 3 + 6 + 3 = 12.
why_wrong: (A) 10 typically comes from dropping two covers, such as 6 above 3 or 15 above 5.
(B) 11 drops exactly one cover.
(D) 14 comes from drawing 1 below every other element, which is the transitive relation rather than the cover relation.
solution.misconception: Drawing an edge for every divisibility pair. That draws the whole relation, not its transitive reduction.
solution.faster: This poset is the Boolean lattice B₃, whose Hasse diagram has 3·2² = 12 edges.
solution.takeaway: Hasse edges count prime-step relations only.

questions.question:
In the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, 18, 36}, how many edges does the Hasse diagram have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The set is closed under divisors, so b covers a exactly when b/a is prime.
steps: Covers of 1: 2 and 3 (both quotients prime) — 2 edges.
Covers of 2 and 3: 4 covers 2; 6 covers 2 and 3 — 3 edges.
Covers of 4 and 6: 12 covers 4 and 6; 18 covers 6 only, because 18/6 = 3 and nothing in P lies between 6 and 18 — 3 edges.
Covers of 12 and 18: 36 covers both — 2 edges.
Total 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 10.
solution.misconception: Adding edges such as 1 to 4, 1 to 6 or 6 to 36. None is a cover: 4/1 = 4 is composite, and 12 lies strictly between 6 and 36.
solution.faster: Lay the poset out by the number of prime factors and join only elements that differ by one prime factor.
solution.takeaway: Count covers by testing each quotient for primality.

questions.question: Consider the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: 36 is the greatest element of P.
The pair {12, 18} has no least upper bound in P.
The least upper bound of {4, 6} in P is 12.
The element 6 covers exactly two elements of P.

solution.concept: In a divisor-closed poset the join is the lcm and the meet is the gcd; the only way a join can fail is if the lcm leaves the set.
steps: 36 is divisible by every element of P, so it is the greatest element. (A) is TRUE.
Upper bounds of {12, 18} in P are the multiples of lcm(12,18) = 36 that lie in P: only 36. So the lub exists and equals 36. (B) is FALSE.
Upper bounds of {4, 6} are 12 and 36; the least is 12. (C) is TRUE.
6/2 = 3 and 6/3 = 2 are prime while 6/1 = 6 is not, so 6 covers exactly 2 and 3. (D) is TRUE.
why_wrong: (B) is the trap: "the only common upper bound sits at the top" is not the same as "there is no least upper bound". A lub may well be the greatest element of the whole poset.
solution.misconception: Expecting the lub to be a small, "nearby" element. When a pair is spread across two branches, the lub is often the top element.
solution.faster: Compute the lcm and check membership in P; do not judge by how far up the diagram the answer sits.
solution.takeaway: In divisor posets, joins are lcms and meets are gcds; failure means the lcm is outside the set.

questions.question: In the divisor lattice D(12) = ({1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, ∣), what is the join (least upper bound) of 4 and 6?
options: 4 and 6 have no join in D(12).

solution.concept: In a divisor lattice the join is the least common multiple, provided it belongs to the lattice; the meet is the greatest common divisor.
steps: Common upper bounds of 4 and 6 are the common multiples: 12, 24, 36, …
Among those, only 12 belongs to D(12).
So the least upper bound is 12.
Answer: 12.
why_wrong: (A) 2 is gcd(4,6), the meet, not the join.
(C) 24 is a common multiple but is not an element of D(12), and 12 is smaller anyway.
(D) is false: 12 is a common upper bound inside the lattice.
solution.misconception: Swapping join and meet. The lcm is the join (an upper bound); the gcd is the meet.
solution.faster: Join = lcm, meet = gcd, then check that the result is an element of the set.
solution.takeaway: In divisor lattices join is lcm and meet is gcd.

questions.question: For which of the following values of n is the divisor lattice D(n) NOT a Boolean lattice?

solution.concept: D(n) is a Boolean lattice exactly when n is squarefree, that is, a product of distinct primes.
steps: If n = p₁p₂…p_k with the primes p_i distinct, then each divisor corresponds to a choice of exponents 0 ≤ e_i ≤ 1 and D(n) is isomorphic to the subset lattice of a k-element set.
6 = 2·3, 30 = 2·3·5 and 210 = 2·3·5·7 are all squarefree, so their divisor lattices are Boolean, on 2, 3 and 4 atoms respectively.
12 = 2²·3 is not squarefree, and D(12) has 6 elements — no Boolean lattice has 6 elements.
Answer: n = 12.
why_wrong: (A), (B) and (D) are squarefree, so their divisor lattices are Boolean lattices.
solution.misconception: Judging by size or by "highly composite". The test is squarefreeness of n, not how many divisors it has.
solution.faster: A Boolean lattice has exactly 2^k elements; |D(n)| = (a₁+1)…(a_k+1) is a power of 2 exactly when every exponent is 1.
solution.takeaway: D(n) is Boolean if and only if n is squarefree.

questions.question:
In the divisor lattice D(36), how many elements have a complement?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: An element x has a complement y when x ∨ y = 1̂ and x ∧ y = 0̂. Since 36 = 2²·3², the lattice is the product of two 3-element chains of exponents.
steps: Since 36 = 2²·3², the lattice is D(36) ≅ C₃ × C₃, a product of two copies of the exponent chain C₃ = {0, 1, 2}.
An element (a,b) has complement (c,d) exactly when a ∨ c = 2, a ∧ c = 0, b ∨ d = 2 and b ∧ d = 0.
Inside C₃ only 0 and 2 have complements: for a = 1, 1 ∨ c = 2 forces c = 2, but then 1 ∧ 2 = 1 ≠ 0.
So each coordinate must be 0 or 2, giving 2 × 2 = 4 elements: 1, 4, 9 and 36.
Check: the complement pairs are (1, 36) and (4, 9).
solution.misconception: Assuming every element of a bounded lattice has a complement. Here 6 is the counterexample: no y satisfies both gcd(6,y) = 1 and lcm(6,y) = 36.
solution.faster: A divisor lattice is complemented only for squarefree n; otherwise decide coordinate by coordinate and multiply.
solution.takeaway: A finite distributive lattice need not be complemented — D(n) is complemented exactly when n is squarefree.

questions.question: In a lattice (L, ≤) with join ∨ and meet ∧, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a for all a, b ∈ L.
a ∨ (a ∧ b) = b for all a, b ∈ L.
If a ≤ b then a ∧ b = a.

solution.concept: The join is the least upper bound and the meet the greatest lower bound; the absorption laws follow directly from those two definitions.
steps: (A) Since a ≤ a ∨ b, the element a ∨ b is an upper bound of both a and a ∨ b, so a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a. TRUE.
(B) Take b < a. Then a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a ∨ b = a, and the claim would give a = b. FALSE.
(C) If a ≤ b then a is a lower bound of both and no larger element is, so a ∧ b = a. TRUE.
(D) Take the five-element lattice 0 < a, b < 1, where a, b are incomparable. It is bounded, but a has no complement: no element both meets it at 0 and joins with it to 1. FALSE.
why_wrong: (B) is the classic slip: the dual absorption law keeps the repeated variable, a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a, on the right-hand side.
(D) confuses "bounded" with "complemented". Boundedness gives a top and a bottom, not complements.
solution.misconception: Treating absorption as if the two variables swapped places. Both laws return the repeated variable, not the other one.
solution.faster: Absorption is immediate from the definitions — no case analysis is needed.
solution.takeaway: Both absorption laws keep the variable that appears twice on the left-hand side.

questions.question: Let R = {(1,2), (2,3)} and S = {(2,3), (3,1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following equals S ∘ R?

solution.concept: S ∘ R consists of the pairs (x,z) for which some y satisfies (x,y) ∈ R and (y,z) ∈ S — that is, of all two-step walks, with the intermediate vertex suppressed.
steps: (1,2) ∈ R and (2,3) ∈ S give (1,3).
(2,3) ∈ R and (3,1) ∈ S give (2,1).
No other pair of R can be followed by a pair of S, so the composition is exactly {(1,3), (2,1)}.
Answer: S ∘ R = {(1,3), (2,1)}.
why_wrong: (B) invents (1,1); there is no two-step walk from 1 back to 1.
(C) is S itself, with the two-step walks not taken.
(D) ignores the two chains that do exist.
solution.misconception: Reading S ∘ R right to left as "apply S then R". In S ∘ R the right-hand factor R acts first.
solution.faster: Follow the arrows: an arrow of R followed by an arrow of S becomes one shortcut edge.
solution.takeaway: In S ∘ R the relation R is applied first, and composition is not commutative in general.

questions.question: Let R and S be relations on a set A. Which of the following statements is TRUE in general?
options: R ∘ S = S ∘ R for all relations R and S.
If R and S are both transitive, then R ∪ S is transitive.
If R and S are both reflexive, then R ∘ S is reflexive.
If R and S are both symmetric, then R ∘ S is symmetric.

solution.concept: Composition preserves reflexivity but not symmetry, and it does not commute; unions preserve neither transitivity nor anything else for free.
steps: (C) If R and S are reflexive then for every a ∈ A both (a,a) ∈ R and (a,a) ∈ S lie in the respective relations, so (a,a) ∈ R ∘ S. TRUE.
(A) fails on A = {1, 2, 3} with R = {(1,2)} and S = {(2,3)}: then S ∘ R = {(1,3)} while R ∘ S = ∅.
(B) fails for the same pair: both relations are transitive, yet R ∪ S = {(1,2), (2,3)} misses (1,3).
(D) fails with R = {(1,2), (2,1)} and S = {(2,3), (3,2)}: then S ∘ R = {(1,3)}, which is not symmetric.
why_wrong: (A) confuses composition with a commutative operation.
(B) assumes transitivity is closed under union; it is closed under intersection, not union.
(D) assumes symmetry survives composition; the composite of two symmetric relations need not be symmetric.
solution.misconception: Believing that any property shared by two relations is inherited by their union or composition. Only some properties are preserved, and by some operations.
solution.faster: Test each claim on the three-element set with single-pair relations — most of these identities collapse immediately.
solution.takeaway: Reflexivity passes to composition; symmetry and transitivity do not.

questions.question:
On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3), (3,4), (4,5), (2,5)}. How many ordered pairs must be added to R to obtain its transitive closure?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The transitive closure is the reachability relation of the digraph of R: (x,y) lies in R⁺ exactly when a directed path of positive length runs from x to y.
steps: Reachability: 1 reaches 2, 3, 4, 5; 2 reaches 3, 4, 5; 3 reaches 4, 5; 4 reaches 5; 5 reaches nothing.
R contains 6 pairs and R⁺ contains 10.
The pairs to add are (1,4), (1,5), (2,4), (3,5) — four of them.
solution.misconception: Stopping after one round of composition, which adds only (1,4) and (2,4) and misses the paths of length 3 and 4.
solution.faster: Do a reachability sweep from each vertex in turn and count the distinct pairs found.
solution.takeaway: The transitive closure is reachability, not one round of composition.

questions.question: How many irreflexive relations are there on a set with three elements?

solution.concept: A relation on a set of n elements is a subset of A × A, which has n² pairs; each property fixes or frees some of those pairs.
steps: For n = 3, the set A × A has 9 ordered pairs.
Irreflexive means the three diagonal pairs (a,a) are all excluded.
The remaining 6 off-diagonal pairs are unconstrained, and each may be in or out.
So the count is 2⁶ = 64.
why_wrong: (A) 2³ = 8 counts subsets of a 3-element set, not relations.
(C) 2⁹ = 512 counts all relations on three elements.
(D) 729 = 3⁶ is not a count of relations at all.
