solution.misconception: Using 2^(n²) for every property. Each constraint removes free pairs and shrinks the exponent.
solution.faster: Count the free pairs first: irreflexive relations on n elements number 2^(n²−n).
solution.takeaway: Compute the exponent as the number of pairs still free, not the size of A × A.

questions.question: How many relations on a set with four elements are both reflexive and antisymmetric?

solution.concept: Reflexivity fixes the diagonal pairs; antisymmetry constrains each unordered off-diagonal pair to at most one direction.
steps: Reflexivity forces all 4 diagonal pairs to be present — 1 way.
The 12 off-diagonal pairs fall into 6 unordered pairs {a, b}.
For each unordered pair, antisymmetry permits exactly three states: neither directed pair, only (a,b), or only (b,a).
Total 3⁶ = 729.
why_wrong: (A) 2⁶ = 64 is the reflexive-and-symmetric count, where each unordered pair is both-or-neither.
(B) 6³ = 216 uses 3 choices but only 3 unordered pairs.
(D) 2¹² = 4096 counts all reflexive relations, ignoring antisymmetry.
solution.misconception: Giving each unordered pair two choices. Antisymmetry leaves three, because either direction may be present or neither.
solution.faster: Reflexive and antisymmetric on n elements number 3^(n(n−1)/2).
solution.takeaway: Reflexive fixes n pairs; antisymmetric contributes 3 options per unordered off-diagonal pair.

questions.question: How many partial orders are there on a set with three elements?

solution.concept: A partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation; on three labelled elements it is best counted by the shape of its Hasse diagram.
steps: Antichain (no comparabilities): 1 order.
Exactly one comparable pair: choose the two elements and the direction, 3 · 2 = 6.
A chain of three: 3! = 6 linear orders.
A V shape: one minimal element below two incomparable elements — choose the minimum, 3 orders.
A Λ shape: one maximal element above two incomparable elements — choose the maximum, 3 orders.
Total 1 + 6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 19.
why_wrong: (A) 12 counts only the chains and the V/Λ shapes.
(C) 27 is the number of reflexive and antisymmetric relations, which ignores transitivity.
(D) 33 double-counts the shapes that are also chains.
solution.misconception: Counting reflexive antisymmetric relations and assuming transitivity is automatic. It is not: {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3)} is reflexive and antisymmetric but not transitive.
solution.faster: Classify by Hasse-diagram shape — antichain, one edge, chain, V, Λ — and multiply by the number of ways to place each shape.
solution.takeaway: Counting posets means counting Hasse-diagram shapes, not pair selections.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about counting relations on a set A with |A| = n are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every relation on A is a subset of A × A, and every subset of A × A is a relation on A.
The number of symmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n+1)/2).
The number of antisymmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n−1)/2).
A reflexive relation on A contains exactly n² − n ordered pairs.

solution.concept: Relations on A correspond exactly to subsets of A × A, so counting relations means counting free choices over the pairs of A × A.
steps: (A) is the definition; the correspondence is a bijection. TRUE.
(B) A symmetric relation is free on the n diagonal pairs and on the n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, so 2^(n + n(n−1)/2) = 2^(n(n+1)/2). TRUE.
(C) fails: antisymmetry allows three states per unordered off-diagonal pair, giving 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2).
(D) fails: reflexivity forces at least the n diagonal pairs and says nothing about the off-diagonal ones, so any number from n up to n² is possible.
why_wrong: (C) swaps the symmetric and antisymmetric formulas. Symmetric uses 2 choices per pair, antisymmetric uses 3.
(D) confuses a lower bound with an exact count.
solution.misconception: Assuming symmetric and antisymmetric relations are counted by the same expression. The antisymmetric count carries an extra factor 2ⁿ.
solution.faster: Symmetric → 2 choices per unordered pair; antisymmetric → 3 choices per unordered pair.
solution.takeaway: Symmetric relations: 2^(n(n+1)/2). Antisymmetric relations: 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2).

questions.question: Let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following equals R ∘ R?

solution.concept: R ∘ R advances every walk by one step: (x,z) lies in R ∘ R exactly when a path of length two runs from x to z.
steps: (1,2) then (2,3) gives (1,3).
(2,3) then (3,1) gives (2,1).
(3,1) then (1,2) gives (3,2).
why_wrong: (B) is R itself. Having (1,2) in the composition would need a y with (1,y) ∈ R and (y,2) ∈ R, and no such y exists.
(C) is the diagonal, which appears only in R³.
(D) ignores the three two-step walks.
solution.misconception: Assuming %s whenever %s is a cycle. Composition shifts the cycle by one step instead of returning it.
solution.faster: For a single directed cycle of length 3, R² is the same cycle rotated and R³ is the diagonal.
solution.takeaway: Here R³ = I_A, so the transitive closure is R ∪ R² ∪ R³ = A × A.
